narrative:
The model estimated a 60.2% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, meaning failure was somewhat more likely than success based on the information available. Because admission depended on that prediction, your application was denied.

The strongest factor behind the denial was your third-year class-rank decile. At 1.00, compared with an accepted-student average of 5.79, this was the most influential item, and it pushed the prediction toward bar-exam failure. Your first-year class-rank decile was the second most important factor; at 1.00 versus an accepted-student average of 6.00, it also pushed toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor. At 2.60, it was below the accepted-student average of 3.23, but here it worked in your favor, pushing the prediction toward passing; it was not enough to outweigh the class-rank signals.

To improve your position, focus on demonstrable academic strengthening. Discuss with an advisor which further coursework or structured bar-readiness preparation could raise your profile, consider retaking the LSAT if a stronger score is realistic, and ask admissions what evidence of improvement they would accept on reapplication. A later application should show concrete gains in the academic areas that drove this decision.
